notable_claims: The Secret Service seized computers from Texas Tech dorms alleging software theft via the Internet.
Revised copyright laws allowed felony charges for pirating more than 10 copies of copyrighted software.
NSFNet backbone access was granted to information providers stating their resources would support research and education.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes various discussions regarding computer law and academic freedom, including a Secret Service raid at Texas Tech University over software piracy. It highlights legal resources for bulletin board operators (SYSLAW), debates on public property rights versus government policy, and NSFNet Acceptable Use Policies. The item also touches upon censorship and the reporting of offensive content to system administrators.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.64

notable_claims: A 1992 copyright law revision allowed felony charges for trading more than 10 pieces of copyrighted software.
The raid involved an expanded right to use forfeiture against computer equipment used in crimes.
classification.summary: The Secret Service raided a Texas Tech University dorm to seize computers from students allegedly using the Internet to trade pirated software. The action highlighted new copyright law revisions that lowered the felony threshold for software piracy and expanded government forfeiture rights over computer hardware.
classification.title: Federal Agents Raid Dorm, Seize Computer Equipment

notable_claims: Law often lags behind technology, leaving sysadmins and sysops in a state of legal uncertainty.
The relationship between a user and a bulletin board is essentially contractual.
Courts had not yet provided definitive answers to many questions regarding the seizure of equipment due to user actions.
classification.summary: A review of the book 'SYSLAW' by Lance Rose and Jonathan Wallace, which examines the intersection of law and computer technology. The text focuses on the legal rights and liabilities of system operators (sysops) regarding censorship, intellectual property, and search and seizure. It highlights the gap between existing statutes and the technological realities of bulletin board systems.
classification.title: Article 2--File 4--SYSLAW (Review #1)

notable_claims: BBSs are analogous to physical printing presses and deserve full First Amendment protection.
The U.S. Secret Service's seizure of BBS hardware raises significant constitutional questions regarding speech and assembly.
Over-cautious sysops may engage in unnecessary self-censorship due to fear of government intervention.
classification.summary: A review of the book 'SYSLAW' by Lance Rose and Jonathan Wallace, which examines the legal liabilities and obligations of Bulletin Board System (BBS) sysops. The text discusses the application of First Amendment protections to electronic speech and the risks posed by government seizures of hardware during hacker crackdowns. It highlights the tension between government intervention and the potential for sysop self-censorship.
classification.title: Article 3--File 5--SYSLAW (Review #2)

notable_claims: System operators may review private e-mail if they believe it is necessary to protect the system from injury or legal seizure.
The contract asserts that users retain rights to original messages, but the operator claims copyright over the 'look and feel' and collective work of message sequences.
classification.summary: This item provides a sample 'Bulletin Board Services Agreement' sourced from SysLaw. The contract outlines the legal and behavioral expectations for users of a Bulletin Board System (BBS), including payment terms, privacy policies, and editorial control. It emphasizes the system operator's right to limit access to prevent illegal activities and protect the system from liability.
classification.title: Article 4--File 6--Model BBS/User Contract (from SYSLAW)

notable_claims: CERT expanded the scope of its advisory to include all systems, not just federal ones.
Access to educational and government computer systems is governed by property rights similar to physical property.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding a CERT advisory based on U.S. Department of Justice guidance concerning keystroke monitoring. The participants debate whether the scope of the advisory applies only to federal systems or all systems regardless of ownership, and how property rights affect access to educational and government computer systems.
classification.title: Article 5--Re: CERT and the Dept. of Justice on keystroke monitoring

identity.subject: Article 5--Re: CERT and the Dept. of Justice on keystroke monitoring

notable_claims: Publicly funded educational sites involve privacy and other rights via academic freedom.
The use of public property should be determined by public policy rather than the preferences of agency heads.
classification.summary: Jyrki Kuoppala responds to Leonard Erickson regarding the nature of public property and access rights to government systems. Kuoppala argues that public property is governed by policy rather than traditional property rights and suggests that academic freedom implies certain privacy rights at educational sites.
classification.title: Article 6--Re: CERT and the Dept. of Justice on keystroke monitoring

identity.subject: Article 6--Re: CERT and the Dept. of Justice on keystroke monitoring

notable_claims: Existing definitions of chain letters may be overly broad, potentially including resumes and jokes.
Two workable definitions of chain letters exist: one based on US Postal regulations and another focusing on distribution for the sake of distribution.
classification.summary: J. S. Greenfield engages in a debate regarding the legal and technical definition of 'chain letters' in the context of electronic communication. The discussion focuses on whether existing definitions are overly broad, potentially encompassing resumes or jokes, and the necessity of precise definitions before taking action.
classification.title: Article 7--Re: Chain letters?

notable_claims: The author argues that absolute definitions of chain letters often fail to capture all 'chain-like' variants.
classification.summary: Tom Leylan responds to J.S. Greenfield regarding the difficulty of establishing a precise definition for 'chain letters.' The exchange focuses on whether definitions should be broad enough to cover variants or narrow enough to exclude items like resumes and jokes.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: Chain letters?

notable_claims: The author claims the US government is a major distributor of child pornography for the purpose of entrapment.
The author argues that photographs should be treated as evidence of a crime rather than a separate crime themselves.
classification.summary: A debate between Douglas Foxvog and Bill Dixon regarding the legal and ethical distinctions between child abuse and the possession or distribution of images. The discussion touches upon government entrapment, the definition of pornography, and whether laws should target the act of abuse rather than the evidence (photos) of that abuse.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: [UPI] "FBI probes computer child porn at Cornell"

identity.subject: Article 9--Re: [UPI] "FBI probes computer child porn at Cornell"

notable_claims: Dialog was initially considered a commercial user of ANS but was later blessed by the NSF as an acceptable research and education user in January 1992.
classification.summary: Gordon Cook questions the current NSFnet Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) regarding commercial information providers. He references a previous dispute where Dialog was initially labeled 'commercial' before being reclassified as a research and education user by the NSF. The post seeks clarification on whether information providers can remain AUP-conformant if they restrict customer use to research and education.
classification.title: Article 10--What *IS* Current AUP Policy for Information Providers?

identity.subject: Article 10--What *IS* Current AUP Policy for Information Providers?

notable_claims: System administrators are the primary authority for determining if material is unsuitable for public medium and for penalizing users' network access.
classification.summary: A user on the newsgroup soc.culture.indian issues a warning to specific posters regarding offensive and racist material. The author threatens to report violators to their respective system administrators to seek penalties or denial of Usenet write access.
classification.title: DEADLINE TO STOP OBSCENE POSTINGS!

identity.subject: Article 11--What *IS* Current AUP Policy for Information Providers?
